claims.text: Controlled heat treatment can form or modify nanoscale short-range order involving corrosion-resistant alloying elements in steels.
Nanoscale short-range order mitigates local corrosion processes in steels.
Short-range ordering reduces defect sites and stabilizes passive films.
Commercial as-cast or as-homogenized steels have a random solid-solution distribution of alloying elements.
Annealing can promote nanoscale short-range ordering relative to a homogenized state.
Electron diffraction and atom probe tomography can be used to identify nanoscale chemical short-range order.
The controlled study will expose samples to simulated chemical-processing or nuclear-power temperatures, corrosive media, and radiation conditions.
The proposed structural mediator consists of nanoscale short-range ordering or clustering, especially Cr-rich clusters.
Ordered alloy configurations occur both at grain boundaries and within grain interiors.
The ordered microstructure decreases local defect density and thereby reduces corrosion-nucleation sites.
The ordered microstructure enhances the formation and stability of passive films.
Reduced corrosion nucleation and more stable passive films impede corrosion propagation relative to a random alloy distribution.
Heat-treated steels with induced short-range order will have significantly lower corrosion rates than compositionally identical homogenized controls.
Heat-treated steels with induced short-range order will show fewer pitting events and less overall corrosion damage than controls.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to steels containing at least 10% Cr and appropriate Ni levels.
The effect may diminish outside the proposed composition range or under conditions far more extreme than normal chemical-processing or nuclear environments.
Potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance, and microscopy will be used to compare corrosion rate, pitting density, and corrosion morphology between treated and control samples.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant corrosion-rate reduction or a noticeable decrease in pitting, despite confirmed ordering, will falsify the hypothesis.
